'''Bryan Ronald Webber''', [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]], [[Fellow of the Institute of Physics|FInstP]] (born 25 July 1943) is a British [[physicist]] and academic. He was a Fellow of [[Emmanuel College, Cambridge]] from 1973 to 2010, and Professor of Theoretical Physics at the [[University of Cambridge]] from 1999 to 2010. He has been awarded the [[Dirac Medal (IOP)|Dirac Medal]] by the [[Institute of Physics]], the [[Sakurai Prize]] by the [[American Physical Society]] and the [[High Energy and Particle Physics Prize]] by the [[European Physical Society]].

==Early life and education==
Webber was born on 25 July 1943 to Frederick Ronald Webber and Iris Evelyn Webber (née Hutchings). He was educated at [[Colston's School]], a [[Private schools in the United Kingdom|private school]] in Bristol.<ref name="Who's Who 2015">{{cite web|title=WEBBER, Prof. Bryan Ronald|url=http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U42174|website=Who's Who 2015|publisher=Oxford University Press|accessdate=2015-07-25|date=November 2014}}</ref> He studied at [[The Queen's College, Oxford]] and graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] (BA) degree in 1964.<ref name="Who's Who 2015" /><ref name="Brief research biography">{{cite web|title=Brief research biography|url=http://www.hep.phy.cam.ac.uk/theory/webber/BryanWebberBio.pdf|website=Department of Physics|publisher=University of Cambridge|accessdate=2015-07-25}}</ref> He then moved to California, United States, to undertake [[postgraduate research]] within the research group of [[Luis Walter Alvarez]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. He completed his [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (PhD) degree in [[experimental particle physics]] in 1969 with a thesis titled ''A test of the ΔS=ΔQ rule in leptonic decays of neutral K mesons''.<ref name="Brief research biography" /><ref>{{cite thesis|title=A test of the [Delta]S=[Delta]Q rule in leptonic decays of neutral K mesons.|url=http://oskicat.berkeley.edu/record=b14427785~S53|website=OskiCat|year = 1969|publisher=University of California, Berkeley|accessdate=2015-07-26|last1 = Webber|first1 = Bryan Ronald}}</ref>

==Research and career==
Webber began his academic career as a [[postdoctoral researcher]] at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory|Lawrence Radiation Laboratory]], California. There, he researched [[strong interaction]] under [[Geoffrey Chew]] from 1969 to 1971.<ref name="Who's Who 2015" /><ref name="Brief research biography" /><ref name="Sakurai Prize" /> He then returned to England, where he joined the [[University of Cambridge]] as a [[research assistant]].<ref name="Who's Who 2015" /> By 1973, he was the only member of staff researching [[particle physics]] theory,<ref name="Brief research biography" /> and was appointed head of the Theoretical High Energy Physics Group at the [[Cavendish Laboratory]].<ref name="Sakurai Prize" />

At university level, he was a [[Scientific demonstration|demonstrator]] from 1973 to 1978. He was a lecturer from 1978 to 1994. He was promoted to [[Reader (academic rank)|reader]] in 1994. He was appointed [[Professor (highest academic rank)|Professor]] of Theoretical Physics in 1999.<ref name="Who's Who 2015" /> He retired in September 2010,<ref>{{cite web|title=QCD in the LHC Era – A meeting in honour of Bryan Webber|url=http://www.hep.phy.cam.ac.uk/news/qcdlhc2010/|website=Department of Physics|publisher=University of Cambridge|accessdate=2015-07-25}}</ref> and was appointed [[Emeritus|Professor Emeritus]].<ref name="Who's Who 2015" />

He was elected a Fellow of [[Emmanuel College, Cambridge]] in 1973.<ref name="Brief research biography" /> He was later made a professorial fellow.<ref name="bio - Department of Physics">{{cite web|title=Professor Bryan Webber|url=http://www.phy.cam.ac.uk/directory/webberb|website=Department of Physics|date=31 July 2013|publisher=University of Cambridge|accessdate=2015-07-25}}</ref> At various times, he was a tutor in physics and was a director of studies at Emmanuel College.<ref name="Brief research biography" /> On retirement in 2010, he was elected a Life Fellow.<ref name="bio - Emmanuel College">{{cite web|title=Professor Bryan Webber|url=http://www.emma.cam.ac.uk/contact/fellows/?id=75#list|publisher=Emmanuel College|accessdate=2015-07-25}}</ref>

==Honours and awards==
In 1987, Webber was elected a [[Fellow of the Institute of Physics]] (FInstP).<ref name="Sakurai Prize" /> In 2001, he was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS).<ref>{{cite web|title=Fellows|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/bryan-webber-12500/|website=Royal Society|accessdate=2026-07-12}}</ref>

In 2008, he was awarded the [[Dirac Medal (IOP)|Dirac Medal]] by the [[Institute of Physics]]. The citation reads:<ref name="Dirac medal">{{cite web|title=2008 Dirac medal|url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/gold/dirac/medallists/page_38433.html|website=Institute of Physics awards|publisher=Institute of Physics|accessdate=2015-07-25|archive-date=15 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170315001255/http://www.iop.org/about/awards/gold/dirac/medallists/page_38433.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
{{blockquote|For his pioneering work in understanding and applying quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the theory of the strong interaction which is one of the three fundamental forces of Nature.}}

In 2012, he was awarded the [[Sakurai Prize|J. J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics]] by the [[American Physical Society]]. The citation reads:<ref name="Sakurai Prize">{{cite web|title=2012 J.J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics Recipient|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Webber&first_nm=Bryan&year=2012|website=Prizes, Awards and Fellowships|publisher=American Physical Society|accessdate=2015-07-25}}</ref>
{{blockquote|For key ideas leading to the detailed confirmation of the Standard Model of particle physics, enabling high energy experiments to extract precise information about Quantum Chromodynamics, electroweak interactions and possible new physics.}}

In 2021, he was awarded the [[High Energy and Particle Physics Prize]] of the [[European Physical Society]]. The short citation reads:<ref>{{cite web|title=The High Energy and Particle Physics Prizes|url=https://eps-hepp.web.cern.ch/hepp-prize-awards.php|publisher=European Physical Society|accessdate=9 Aug 2026}}</ref>
{{blockquote|For the conception, development and realisation of parton shower Monte Carlo simulations}}
He received the award together with [[Torbjörn Sjöstrand]], who was also a co-recipient of the Sakurai Prize.
